none: English translation only; no explanatory claims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb’s subject is unstated, but the following verses identify the Prophet as the one who frowned.
rows.anchor: the succeeding verses that the Prophet (sws) is its subject

rows.speaker: All exegetes
rows.claim: All exegetes agree that the blind man was the poor companion ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm.
rows.anchor: All exegetes are unanimous that the verse

rows.speaker: some narratives
rows.claim: Some narratives describe the Prophet speaking with Quraysh leaders when Ibn Umm Maktūm entered without recognizing the meeting’s delicate nature; the Prophet disliked the interruption.
rows.anchor: It is mentioned in some narratives that one day the Prophet (sws) was talking to one of the leaders of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s displeasure was not due to the man’s poverty or blindness; he may have feared losing a chance to persuade Quraysh leaders, who might reject a gathering of poor companions.
rows.anchor: This dislike on the part of the Prophet (sws) of course could not have been because he was poor or blind

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh leaders objected that the Prophet’s companions were poor and destitute, treating this as evidence against his prophethood.
rows.anchor: his companions were the poverty-stricken and the destitute. They regarded this to be an argument against his prophethood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet may also have feared that arrogant leaders would disrespect his dear companion, causing still greater distress.
rows.anchor: he feared that these leaders being inebriated with their superiority

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God used the accidental incident to teach the Prophet to focus on companions eager for reform, rather than pampering indifferent people.
rows.anchor: used by the Almighty for the instruction and education of the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet initially concentrated on Quraysh because he was directed to warn his near family, and their conversion could open Arabia to Islam.
rows.anchor: as is evident from the following verse:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Quraysh’s arrogance made reform unlikely, pursuing them cost time better spent educating poor believers, so the incident enabled a change in strategy.
rows.anchor: the time being wasted on them was at the cost of poor Muslims who had already embraced faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unnamed addressee leaves readers wondering who the incident concerns, while “you know” indicates that the Prophet is being addressed and neglects his own flock for lost sheep.
rows.anchor: shows that this incident relates to the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The initial lack of a specified addressee reassures readers; naming the Prophet would suggest the rebuke was for rudeness toward a blind man, which was not its cause.
rows.anchor: had the addressee been specified, this rebuke would have become very severe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The later direct address identifies the rebuke’s occasion: the Prophet exceeded his duty through zeal, as prophets can overreach from devotion; Moses likewise arrived early at Ṭūr from eagerness to please God.
rows.anchor: this rebuke was not because the Prophet (sws) was in anyway slack in fulfilling an obligation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s devotion to persuading Quraysh leaders led him to neglect his own comfort and risk leaving little time to teach poor believers; he had assumed more than God required.
rows.anchor: he had taken much more upon himself than the responsibility that was imposed upon him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording suggests the blind man’s arrival dismayed the Prophet because he feared it would offend Quraysh vanity, although he was neglecting a more worthy student.
rows.anchor: he had become indifferent to a true student

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messengers’ mission is to purify followers spiritually; those seeking reform deserve attention, while people without that urge do not advance the preaching mission despite worldly importance.
rows.anchor: the real objective of the messengers of God is to spiritually purify their followers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earnest seeker is marked by a desire for inner purification and by benefiting from reminders.
rows.anchor: he is desirous of his inner-purification and he is one who benefits from being reminded

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True students either come with a question and seek guidance or come to hear instruction and learn from answers to others; either purpose makes them worthy of attention.
rows.anchor: there were two types of people among them: one, people who had a question regarding their instruction and training

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People who come only to be pampered should stay home and await their fate.
rows.anchor: As far as people who want to be pampered are concerned, they should sit at home

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God-fearing people who seek reform merit the Prophet’s attention and constitute his responsibility.
rows.anchor: Only the God-fearing who have the urge to reform themselves are worthy of his attention

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form taṣaddā derives from ṣadad, meaning parallel or opposite; its morphological change is regular, and it describes anxiety to convince indifferent people.
rows.anchor: it means “parallel” and “opposite.” The change in its morphological form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s duty is to warn of the Hereafter and communicate Islam, not to ensure that people become Muslims or to overburden himself over their refusal.
rows.anchor: the real responsibility of the Prophet (sws) is to warn people of the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word yasʿā means to act zealously, not necessarily to run; in 62:9 it means turning eagerly to God’s word, like a thirsty person approaching a fountain.
rows.anchor: means to do something with zeal and enthusiasm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indifferent are absorbed in worldly pleasures and do not consider the afterlife, whereas those who fear meeting God are receptive; the Prophet pursued the former while neglecting the latter.
rows.anchor: there are people who fear meeting God in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent admonition to the Prophet indirectly condemns unworthy Quraysh leaders and redirects his efforts toward poor Muslims who had embraced faith.
rows.anchor: the admonition sounded in these verses which apparently seems directed at the Prophet (sws) is actually directed at the unworthy leaders of the Qurasyh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet was corrected for taking on more than his assigned responsibility, not for neglecting it; 26:3 offers another affectionate admonition of this kind.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) has not been checked for being irresponsible in any manner

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poor Muslims who fear God are Islam’s real asset, unlike affluent people whose hearts lack God-fearingness, so the Prophet should prioritize them.
rows.anchor: the real asset of Islam are the poor Muslims who are instilled with the fear of God

rows.speaker: Far āhī
rows.claim: Farāhī’s shepherd analogy shows that an apparent rebuke of a conscientious shepherd is actually aimed at a foolish lost sheep; likewise, Quraysh are indirectly rebuked while the Prophet is treated affectionately.
rows.anchor: Im ām Ham īd al-D īn Far āhī in his exegesis on S ūrah ‘Abas

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet need only communicate the Qur’an’s reminder and warn of consequences; he must not force it on or pamper people who reject it.
rows.anchor: the responsibility of the Prophet (sws) is to only communicate this reminder to people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun’s antecedent is dhikr in verse 4, referring to the Qur’an; the masculine form points to its real meaning, and similar usage occurs in earlier sūrahs.
rows.anchor: Examples of such usage can be seen in previous sūrahs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Any reproach in the address is affectionate and means the Prophet assumed more responsibility than was assigned to him.
rows.anchor: if there is an element of rebuke in this address it is affection-oriented

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A clause is suppressed after “whoever wishes”: the reminder can be accepted or ignored, as 18:29 similarly permits belief or disbelief.
rows.anchor: then whoever wants can profess belief and whoever wants can profess disbelief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guarded tablet is a priceless divine treasure accessible only by God’s leave and bestowed on the Prophet for the worthy; he should not cast pearls before a swine.
rows.anchor: he should only present it before those who are worthy of it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guarded tablet is a powerful, priceless treasure protected by angels.
rows.anchor: it is a powerful and priceless treasure

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣaḥīfa means a written page and its plural can mean a book; here it denotes the guarded tablet, a priceless treasure accessible only by God’s leave and bestowed on the Prophet for the worthy.
rows.anchor: it refers to the guarded tablet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pages’ raised quality denotes exalted meaning and status, as in 43:4, which describes the original book as exalted and wise.
rows.anchor: The former refers to exaltedness both in meaning and status

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their purification means the Qur’an is secure from devils; 56:78–79 calls it a guarded book accessible only to the pure, with angels as its trustworthy custodians.
rows.anchor: is to bring to light the fact

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of the pages as held in scribes’ hands identifies the keepers of the secure book and contrasts with the negative statement in 56:79.
rows.anchor: delineate the characteristics of scribes in whose custody this secure book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Safara, plural of sāfir, means reader and scribe, combining reading and writing; its original sense was writing and later broadened.
rows.anchor: It connotes both reading and writing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final adjectives describe the custodians as high-status, honorable, obedient, faithful, responsible, and trustworthy, incapable of dishonesty or allowing devils access.
rows.anchor: This adjective further highlights their

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger delivering revelation is powerful, honored, obeyed, and trustworthy, as described in 81:19–21.
rows.anchor: This is the word brought by a noble messenger; he is endued with great power

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an and its custodians’ attributes require the Prophet and his Companions to preach with honor and dignity rather than beg or implore.
rows.anchor: it should be presented with honour and dignity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The archangel and the scribes entrusted with revelation have lofty character and integrity; earthly transmitters are selected for corresponding qualities.
rows.anchor: only those people in this earth are selected to transmit and deliver this word of God who have the same qualities and attributes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Brief reminders about creation, life’s sources, death, and resurrection expose the transience of arrogant pride and point to Judgment.
rows.anchor: In these verses, the pride and vanity of these people is condemned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh assumed their worldly respect and leadership would continue after Judgment; 70:36–39 challenges their expectation of Paradise.
rows.anchor: the warning sounded by the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Across the Qur’an, human creation and its phases are used to establish resurrection; Islahi says this topic appears in various styles.
rows.anchor: This topic is mentioned in the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being created from an impure drop gives people no grounds to boast of purity, superiority, or entitlement to Paradise.
rows.anchor: boast of their purity and superiority

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi illustrates the resurrection argument with 23:12–16’s account of human creation from clay through successive stages and restoration after death.
rows.anchor: And We first created man from an essence of clay

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Judgment will evaluate people’s good and evil deeds, select those who meet its standards, and cast down those who fail them.
rows.anchor: evaluates the good and evil done by him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s measuring, planning, and easing of human creation and life stages show providence has a purpose, which entails judgment and recompense.
rows.anchor: it is essential that a day come wherein it judges him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relevant term describes life’s gradual stages from childhood through youth to old age; like the moon’s phases in 36:39, these attest to divine power and purposeful creation, resurrection, and judgment.
rows.anchor: this word directs our attention to the various stages of life through which he gradually passes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes commonly restrict God’s easing to delivery for mother and child, which the author accepts but broadens to providential ease from womb and birth through nourishment and human activity.
rows.anchor: our exegetes generally say that it refers to the easing out which providence has ordained in the body of the mother and her child for delivery

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God eases both material and spiritual life; following the guided path avoids stumbling, but misuse of free will leads to ruin.
rows.anchor: If he treads this path, he will never stumble

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Death is the final and unavoidable life phase; the word for burial subtly depicts the dead as entrusted to earth’s custody, to be reclaimed.
rows.anchor: no one can escape death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nashr means opening, dispersing, or raising anew; whenever God wills, He can easily raise the dead, just as He fashioned a person from a drop in the womb.
rows.anchor: This He will do with the greatest

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 87:2–3 describes God perfecting creation, setting destinies, and giving guidance; 91:7–10 says the soul receives moral direction and succeeds through purification.
rows.anchor: the soul and the morals ordained in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke parallels 80:17: human existence and providence corroborate the Judgment that obdurate people deny, since God will not leave a favored person unaccountable.
rows.anchor: This verse is in parallel to the above quoted verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about not fulfilling what the Lord commanded means the case for Judgment has been fully taught, yet the obstinate remain indifferent; the command includes both natural moral truths and revelation.
rows.anchor: all the directives which are among self-evident realities of human nature and also the directives which the Almighty has revealed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If earlier proofs fail to persuade, reflection on food and the rain that sustains it shows resurrection is easy for God and that providential favor entails accountability.
rows.anchor: Man should only reflect on the food on which his life depends

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sincere reflection on abundant, varied food and rain shows that resurrection is easy for God and that people will answer for their duties toward divine favors.
rows.anchor: The very rain which is a means of his subsistence practically demonstrates this fact

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain and opened earth pores are signs of God’s power and mercy; no one else can provide these conditions on which the earth’s benefits depend.
rows.anchor: Neither is anyone else in the position to send down rain from the skies nor to open the pores of the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The food argument parallels the creation argument: both establish resurrection’s possibility, cite providential signs, and culminate in accountability and reward or punishment.
rows.anchor: the sequence of premises in the argument presented is the same
